lead: A treebank is a corpus of sentences with hand-checked syntax trees attached, so grammar writing becomes counting: read the rules off the trees and count them. Raw treebank rules are untidy — long right-hand sides, mixed terminals and nonterminals, unit rules — and the CYK parser wants them in Chomsky normal form, where every rule is A → BC or A → a. This chapter covers both halves: how trees turn into grammar rules, and how any grammar is rewritten into CNF without changing the language it generates.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for rules, derivations and parse trees.

sections.h3: Treebanks: a grammar hiding in annotated sentences

blocks.text: A treebank is a corpus of sentences, each stored with its syntactic annotation — a parse tree drawn and checked by a human. The best known is the Penn Treebank, built from Wall Street Journal articles. In a constituency treebank a sentence appears as a bracketed tree: (S (NP (DT the) (NN boy)) (VP (VBZ eats) (NP (DT a) (NN sweet)))). The inner nodes are phrase labels: S for sentence, NP for noun phrase, VP for verb phrase. The leaves are words, each sitting under a part-of-speech tag: DT determiner, NN noun, VBZ verb.

A dependency treebank stores the same sentence differently: every word points to its head word and carries a label for the relation, so boy is the nsubj (subject) of eats. Universal Dependencies is the open collection most projects use, and it covers Hindi, Tamil and Marathi among its languages. Which kind you need depends on the parser you will run; see 3.6.

A treebank is also a grammar. Every local tree — one node with its immediate children — is one rule: the subtree (NP (DT the) (NN boy)) gives NP → DT NN. Read every local tree in the corpus and you have a grammar with counts. A rule seen 40,000 times is core English; a rule seen once may be an annotation slip. A rule that never occurs in the treebank will never be proposed by a parser trained on it — the sparse-data problem, handled by smoothing in 3.5.

Chomsky normal form (CNF) is a restricted shape for a context-free grammar: every rule is either A → BC, with exactly two nonterminals on the right, or A → a, with exactly one terminal. A, B, C are nonterminals; a is a terminal, that is, a word. Nothing else is allowed: no right-hand side of three or more symbols, no rule mixing a word with a nonterminal, no unit rule A → B, no empty rule A → ε. The one exception is S → ε, allowed only when the empty string is in the language.

Why bother: CYK (3.3) fills a table over spans of the sentence, and for each span it tries every split into two smaller spans. Binary rules make that loop uniform — one split, one rule, one lookup. Every CFG has an equivalent CNF grammar: the same set of sentences, with different rule shapes.

items: Isolate terminals. A word that shares a right-hand side with nonterminals, as in S → NP VP ., gets a nonterminal of its own: PERIOD → ., and the rule becomes S → NP VP PERIOD. Reuse one helper nonterminal per word, not a fresh one per occurrence.
Binarise long rules. A → B1 B2 … Bn with n ≥ 3 becomes A → B1 X1, X1 → B2 X2, up to X(n−2) → B(n−1) Bn. Keep the left-to-right order of the symbols. One rule of length n becomes n − 1 rules.

Remove ε rules. Find the nullable nonterminals, those that can derive the empty string, add versions of the rules with the nullable symbols dropped, then delete the ε rules. If the empty string is in the language, add a fresh start symbol with S0 → S and S0 → ε.

Remove unit rules. Delete A → B by copying every rule of B under A, and repeat until no unit rule remains. Break cycles such as A → B with B → A first, keeping one direction. Remove ε rules first, because dropping nullable symbols can create unit rules; then remove unit rules as the last shape-fixing step, and check once more that no unit rule appeared.

blocks.text: The language does not change. Only the derivations change: a sentence that took one step now takes several, and the parse tree gains helper nodes. Binarising and isolating terminals are linear: a rule of n symbols becomes n − 1 rules. Unit-rule removal copies rules and can grow the grammar polynomially in the worst case. The language never changes; only the size and the derivations do. Greibach normal form is the other named form: there every rule is A → aα, one terminal first and then any number of nonterminals.

figure.caption: The only rule longer than two symbols splits at its first symbol: S keeps NP and hands VP PP to a new helper nonterminal X1, kept in the original order. The grammar goes from 10 rules to 11 and generates exactly the same sentences.

spec.title: S → NP VP PP becomes two binary rules
spec.aria: One rule of three symbols, S → NP VP PP, out of a 10-rule grammar, splits into S → NP X1 and X1 → VP PP using one new nonterminal X1, giving an 11-rule grammar with the same sentences.

examples.question: Convert this grammar to Chomsky normal form and give the number of rules before and after: S → NP VP PP; NP → Det N; VP → V NP; PP → P NP; Det → the | a; N → boy | girl; V → ate; P → with.
steps: Write each alternative as its own rule and count: S → NP VP PP, NP → Det N, VP → V NP, PP → P NP, Det → the, Det → a, N → boy, N → girl, V → ate, P → with. That is 10 rules.
Step 1, isolate terminals: the, a, boy, girl, ate and with each already stand alone in a lexical rule, so no rule mixes a word with nonterminals. Nothing to do.
Step 2, binarise: only S → NP VP PP is longer than two symbols. Add X1 → VP PP and rewrite S → NP X1. One rule is replaced by two, so one new nonterminal and a net gain of one rule.
Steps 3 and 4: no unit rules A → B and no ε rules exist, so nothing is removed and no new start symbol is needed.
Count the result: 10 − 1 + 2 = 11 rules. The single helper node X1 keeps the children in the order NP, VP, PP, so every yield is unchanged.
examples.answer: The CNF grammar has 11 rules against 10 before, adds one nonterminal X1, and generates exactly the same sentences.
examples.check:
before = [("S", ["NP", "VP", "PP"]), ("NP", ["Det", "N"]),
          ("VP", ["V", "NP"]), ("PP", ["P", "NP"]),
          ("Det", ["the"]), ("Det", ["a"]),
          ("N", ["boy"]), ("N", ["girl"]),
          ("V", ["ate"]), ("P", ["with"])]
long_rules = [r for r in before if len(r[1]) > 2]
new_rules = sum(len(r[1]) - 1 for r in long_rules)
after = len(before) - len(long_rules) + new_rules
print(len(before))
print(after)
print(new_rules - len(long_rules))

traps: Binarising out of order: A → B C D must become A → B X, X → C D, never A → B X, X → D C, because swapping the two groups changes the word order of every yield.
Adding S → NP X1 and forgetting X1 → VP PP: a nonterminal with no rule of its own can never be rewritten, so the sentence is lost.
Deleting a unit rule like VP → V without copying V's rules under VP, or forgetting the fresh start symbol S0 → S, S0 → ε when the empty string is in the language.
Believing CNF changes the language. It changes derivations and tree shape only; the set of sentences is exactly the same.
Creating a new helper nonterminal for every occurrence of the same word instead of reusing one, which bloats the grammar for no reason.

quiz.q: Define a treebank in one sentence.
quiz.a: A corpus of sentences stored with their syntactic annotation — constituency trees or head-to-dependent links — checked by human annotators.

quiz.q: State the two rule shapes allowed in Chomsky normal form.
quiz.a: A → BC, with two nonterminals on the right, and A → a, with one terminal. The only extra rule permitted is S → ε when the empty string is in the language.

quiz.q: Why does the CYK algorithm prefer a grammar in CNF?
quiz.a: CYK splits every span into two parts. Binary rules mean each split is one table lookup and every rule has the same length, so the inner loop is uniform instead of handling rules of length 2, 3 or 4 separately.

quiz.q: Convert S → A B C D to CNF and count the rules it becomes.
quiz.a: S → A X1, X1 → B X2, X2 → C D. One rule of four symbols becomes three rules, using two new nonterminals X1 and X2.

quiz.q: Convert VP → to V NP to CNF, where to is a word and V, NP are nonterminals.
quiz.a: Step 1 gives TO → to and VP → TO V NP. Step 2 binarises: VP → TO X, X → V NP. Three rules in place of one, all binary or lexical.

quiz.q: A treebank gives VP → V NP 40,000 times and VP → V NP PP 12 times. What do the two counts tell you, and what danger do they carry?
quiz.a: The first pattern is common English and the second is rare but real. The rare rule is fine as a grammar rule, yet a model that estimates probabilities from these counts will give it a tiny probability and may never select it; rare and unseen rules need smoothing, covered in 3.5.

quiz.q: Why must unit rules be removed before a grammar can be used by CYK?
quiz.a: A unit rule A → B produces no split into two parts, so CYK has no place for it; worse, a cycle A → B with B → A can loop forever. Substituting B's rules under A removes the problem and keeps the language.

beyond: Not for the exam. Treebanks are the training data behind statistical and neural parsers, so the Penn Treebank and Universal Dependencies are the names to search first. CoNLL-U is the plain-text file format Universal Dependencies uses, and reading one file teaches more than any description. Modern neural parsers predict trees directly and rarely build CNF grammars, yet the same span-splitting idea returns in span-based constituency parsers and inside attention-based syntax models. Unsupervised grammar induction — learning rules with no treebank at all — is an active research problem. Search terms: Universal Dependencies, CoNLL-U, Penn Treebank, grammar induction.
